まって ください — Wait, please!
You learn the three verb groups and the ～て form: you use it to ask for something politely (～てください) and to link actions (“I get up, wash and go out”).
I take; I take (a photo) (→ とって)
I teach, I tell (→ おしえて)
(シャワー を) I take a shower (→ あびて)
I go out, I leave (→ でて)
In the morning I get up, take a shower and go out.
To recognise the three groups of Japanese verbs.
To form the ～て form from the ～ます form, for every group.
To ask for something politely: ～て ください.
To link several actions in order: ～て、～て、～ます.
To use survival phrases: もう いちど / ゆっくり … ください.
After the karaoke evening, Hanako asks Mihai to teach her the guitar. The first lesson takes place in Mihai’s new flat.
Hello. Sorry, I’m a little late.
Wow, what a spacious room. Oh, a cat!
It’s the cat from next door. Because the window was open, it came in.
Well, let’s get started. Please use this guitar.
OK. How do I hold it? Please show me.
Hold here with your right hand and press this with your left hand.
Sorry, say it once more, please. Slowly, please.
With your right hand, hold, here. With your left hand, press, this.
Yes, good. Now watch my hand and play the same.
(Twang) …It’s a bit of a strange sound.
It’s fine. Press a little harder with your fingers.
You’re good! Please practise for ten minutes every day.
Yes! Er, may I take a photo? With my teacher.

Many ～て forms have a double pause: mat-te, tot-te, it-te. Stop for a moment before “te”, as in サッカー.
Verbs in -みます, -びます, -にます make ～んで: yon-de, non-de. Hold the ん for a whole beat.
The u in く is swallowed: “k’dasai”. Japanese people speak quickly: “chotto matte k’dasai”.
So far you’ve only used the ～ます form, which is the same for all verbs. For the ～て form you need to know which GROUP a verb belongs to. Look at the sound before ます:
before ます there’s an -i sound: き, ぎ, し, ち, に, び, み, り, い
before ます there’s an -e sound (or a few -i sounds, as exceptions)
Trap: みます, おきます, あびます, います have -i before ます, but they’re group 2. Learn them as exceptions. And かえります (I go back) and はいります (I enter) look like group 2, but they’re group 1!
Group 2: drop ます and add て. That’s it!
Group 3: します → して, きます → きて.

The most important exception: いきます (I go) → いって, not “いいて”!
Don’t try to learn them all today. The app will give you the ～て form next to every new verb (as in this chapter’s word list). In 2–3 weeks they’ll come naturally.
4. The polite request: ～て ください
The ～て form + ください = “please do…”. It’s the most common way to ask for something politely.
Survival phrases for any conversation: もう いちど いって ください (say it once more), ゆっくり はなして ください (speak more slowly), えいご で いって ください (say it in English).
Bonus: ～て も いい です か = “may I…?” (is it allowed?). しゃしん を とって も いい です か = May I take a photo?
5. Several actions in order: ～て、～て、～ます
To say “I do X, then Y, then Z”, put all the verbs in the ～て form except the LAST one. The last verb shows the tense (present or past) for the whole sentence.
In the morning I get up, wash my face and have breakfast.
Yesterday I went to the shop and bought a shirt.
Don’t put ～ました on every verb! Only the last one takes the tense. Correct: いって、かいました. Wrong: いきました、かいました (it sounds like a robotic list).

ゆきさん の あさ — Yuki’s morning
The teacher on the Japanese course asked the students to describe their mornings. Yuki wrote the text as a model for Mihai.
Every morning I get up at six and open the window.
Then I take a shower and wash my face and brush my teeth.
I listen to the news from Japan on the radio and make breakfast.
Breakfast is rice and miso soup. I learned it from my mother.
At eight I leave home and take the metro to university.
On the metro I read a book in Spanish.
But yesterday I overslept! I got dressed in a hurry and left without eating anything.
Mihai, tell me what your morning is like too.

おにぎり の じゅぎょう — The onigiri lesson
It’s Friday, club day. Today the teacher is Kenji.
On the table there’s rice, nori seaweed, salt and pickled plums.
Everyone washed their hands and put on an apron.
“Then wet your hands a little with water and put on some salt.”
“Why do we use water?” asked Carlos.
“So the rice doesn’t stick to your hands.”
“Then take some rice and put a pickled plum in the middle.”
“Make it into a triangle. Don’t squeeze it hard. Gently.”
Kenji’s onigiri was a perfect triangle.
But everyone else’s came out in all sorts of shapes.
Carlos’s was round, like a ball.
Sofia’s was flat like a pizza. “It’s an Italian onigiri!”
Ana’s was small, shaped like a cute little star.
Mihai tried his very best. But lots of rice stuck to his hands.
Everyone laughed. Mihai laughed too and washed his hands again.
At that moment the door opened and the lady from reception came in.
The lady’s name is Mrs Suzuki. She was Japanese!
“Oh, onigiri? How nostalgic! Please show me.”
Mrs Suzuki took Mihai’s hands and they shaped one together.
“Like this, and like this… there, done.”
In Mihai’s hands was a perfect triangular onigiri.
“Mrs Suzuki, thank you! Where did you learn?”
“I learned from my mother. Fifty years ago.”
At the end, everyone ate onigiri together.
The round ones, the flat ones and the stars were all delicious.
Tama was waiting under the table. But she didn’t like the pickled plums.
“Next week, please be our teacher too, Mrs Suzuki!” said Yuki.
What has to be done first?
Write the ～て form. You can write in kana or romaji.
